summary: Describes a standard mechanism for clients to bootstrap using the iSCSI protocol. The aim is for boot clients to obtain the information needed to open a session with the iSCSI boot server. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A computer with no disk inside must find a storage server on the network before it can start up. This RFC lists the steps: get an address, learn the name and the address of the server, then open an iSCSI session (SCSI storage commands carried over TCP) and boot from it.

questions: what is the iscsi root path string
what are the stages of iscsi boot
how does an iscsi client find its boot server
subtitle: How a computer with no disk of its own finds its iSCSI boot server and collects the information it needs to boot.

tldr.problem: A client with no disk of its own may power on with no network address, no name for the storage server, and not even the software needed to speak iSCSI.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four stages. The client loads iSCSI software if it needs it, asks BOOTP or DHCP for its address and a Root Path string, uses a discovery service to turn the target name into an address, then opens an iSCSI session and boots.
tldr.outcome: A client can boot from a server anywhere it can open an iSCSI session, but the RFC leaves the iSCSI command sequence to each implementor and warns that iSCSI boot must be turned on deliberately by an administrator.

facts.label: LUN text form
facts.value: Four groups of four hexadecimal digits

today: RFC 4173 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2005 that has since been updated by RFC 7146, and it has not been obsoleted. The text itself leaves the iSCSI command sequence for the boot stage to each implementor.

sections.title: Booting From a Disk on the Network
sections.content:
SCSI, the Small Computer Systems Interface, is a popular family of protocols for communicating with input and output devices, especially storage devices. It works as a request and response protocol, with a standard architecture and componentized command sets for different device classes.

iSCSI, the Internet Small Computer Systems Interface, is a transport protocol for SCSI that operates on top of TCP. Its role comes from the way systems changed: the system interconnect moved from a shared bus to a switched network, and IP networks meet the architectural and performance requirements of transporting SCSI.

Many diskless clients bootstrap off remote SCSI devices. Such diskless entities are lightweight, space efficient and power conserving, and they are increasingly popular in various environments.

This memo describes a standard mechanism for enabling clients to bootstrap themselves using the iSCSI protocol. The goal is narrow: let an iSCSI boot client obtain the information it needs to open an iSCSI session with the iSCSI boot server. Some of that information may not be available at the outset, so the memo describes steps to obtain it. The steps are named after where the information comes from: the software stage, the DHCP stage, the discovery service stage and the boot stage.

The memo also surveys the related work it builds on: RARP and its DRARP extensions for network address discovery, TFTP for transporting a boot image, BOOTP for configuration information, DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 for dynamic host configuration, and the Service Location Protocol for locating services.
sections.plainLanguage: iSCSI carries SCSI storage commands over TCP, so a computer can reach a disk on the network. This RFC explains how a computer with no disk of its own collects the few facts it needs before it can use one.

sections.title: What a Boot Client Needs
sections.content:
The RFC lists five requirements.

First, there must be no restriction of network topology between the boot client and the boot server beyond the restriction already in effect for establishing the iSCSI session. A client can therefore boot from a server behind gateways or firewalls, as long as an iSCSI session can be established between them.

Second, the minimum information a client needs in order to contact a boot server is its own IP address, either IPv6 or IPv4, the server's iSCSI Target Name, and the mandatory iSCSI initiator capability. These assumptions hold when the default LUN for the boot process is 0 and the default port for the boot server is the well-known iSCSI port, but both may be overridden at the time of configuration. The LUN, the logical unit number, picks which disk inside the server to use.

Third, it is possible for the client to have none of that information or capability when it starts. Fourth, the client should be able to complete a boot without user intervention, for the boots that happen during an unattended power-up, while there should still be a mechanism for the user to enter values so as to bypass stages of the boot protocol. Fifth, additional protocol software, for example BOOTP or DHCP, may be necessary if the minimum information is not provided.

More information may be required at each stage of the boot process, so the rest of the memo describes where that extra information comes from.
sections.plainLanguage: To reach a storage server, a client needs three things: its own IP address, the name of the server, and the software that speaks iSCSI. The client may start with none of them, so the RFC also asks that the boot finish without a person answering questions.

sections.title: The Software Stage
sections.content:
Some iSCSI boot clients lack the resources to boot up with the mandatory iSCSI initiator capability. Such clients may choose to obtain iSCSI initiator software from a boot server.

Many established protocols already allow this kind of service, so that clients can load software images. BOOTP and DHCP servers, for example, have the capability to provide the locations of servers that can serve software images when a boot client requests them.

The RFC does not recommend any of those protocols. The final decision about which boot protocol is used to load the iSCSI initiator software is left to the discretion of the implementor.
sections.plainLanguage: A very small computer may not have the iSCSI code built in. The RFC allows it to fetch that code from a server first, and leaves the choice of how to fetch it to the maker of the client.

sections.title: The DHCP Stage and the Root Path Option
sections.content:
Three pieces of information are needed to use an iSCSI boot server: the IP address of the client, either IPv4 or IPv6; the IP transport endpoint for the iSCSI Target Port of the boot server, which for TCP means an IP address and a TCP port number; and the eight-byte LUN structure identifying the logical unit within the boot server.

At boot time, all or none of this information may be stored in the client. If the client already has all of it, it may proceed directly to the boot stage. A client that does not know its IP address at power-on may acquire one via BOOTP, the Bootstrap Protocol, or DHCP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, in version 4 or version 6, or via IPv6 address autoconfiguration. DHCP settings, such as the RA settings in DHCPv6, may prohibit the use of DHCP in distributing iSCSI boot information, in which case the DHCP stage cannot be used. Unless the RFC specifies otherwise, BOOTP and DHCP fields such as the client ID and gateway information are used in an identical way as in applications other than iSCSI.

A BOOTP or DHCP server MAY instruct an iSCSI client how to reach its boot device by using the variable-length option named Root Path. The use of the option field is reserved for iSCSI boot use by prefacing the string with iscsi:. The option field consists of a UTF-8 string with the following composition:

"iscsi:"<servername>":"<protocol>":"<port>":"<LUN>":"<targetname>

The servername, protocol, port and LUN fields are optional and should be left blank if there are no corresponding values. The targetname field is not optional and MUST be provided.

  • servername: a valid domain name, a literal IPv4 address or a literal IPv6 address, following the specifications of the URI Specification. Servername compression MUST NOT be used in this field.
  • protocol: the decimal representation of the IANA-approved string for the transport protocol to be used for iSCSI. If the field is left blank, the default value is assumed to be 6 for TCP. The transport protocol MUST have been approved for use in iSCSI, and currently the only approved protocol is TCP.
  • port: the decimal representation of the port on which the iSCSI boot server is listening. If it is not specified, the port defaults to the well-known iSCSI port.
  • LUN: the hexadecimal representation of the LU number. If the field is blank, LUN 0 is assumed. If the field is not blank, the representation MUST be divided into four groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by a hyphen, and digits above 9 may be in either case. An example is 4752-3A4F-6b7e-2F99. At most three leading zeros may be omitted in any group, so 6734-9-156f-127 is equivalent to 6734-0009-156f-0127. Trailing groups that contain only the digit 0 may be omitted along with the preceding hyphen, so 4186-9 is equivalent to 4186-0009-0000-0000. Other concise representations of the LUN field MUST NOT be used.
  • targetname: an iSCSI Name, as defined by the iSCSI standard, that uniquely identifies an iSCSI target. The approved characters are stated in the iSCSI String Profile document.

SCSI targets are allowed to present different LU numberings to different SCSI initiators, so a target may export several different logical units to several different initiators as their respective LUN 0.

If the servername field is provided by BOOTP or DHCP, that field is used with the other associated fields to contact the boot server in the boot stage. If the servername field is not provided, the targetname field is used in the discovery service stage instead.
sections.plainLanguage: In this stage the client learns its own address, the address and port of the storage server, and which disk inside that server it wants. A BOOTP or DHCP server can pass all of that in one text string that starts with iscsi:.

sections.title: The Discovery Service Stage
sections.content:
This stage is required if the BOOTP or DHCP server is unaware of any iSCSI boot servers, or if it cannot provide the minimum information required to connect to the boot server other than the target name.

The discovery service may be based on the Service Location Protocol, SLP, in which case it is an instantiation of the SLP Service or Directory Agent. Alternatively it may be based on the Internet Storage Name Service, iSNS, in which case it is an instantiation of the iSNS Server.

When the client has obtained the target name in the DHCP stage, it queries the SLP discovery service using query string 1 of the iSCSI Target Concrete Service Type Template, to resolve the target name to an IP address and a port number. Alternatively it may query the iSNS discovery service with a Device Attribute Query that uses the target name as the query parameter. Once that information is obtained, the client proceeds to the boot stage.

The port number from the discovery service may conflict with the one from the DHCP stage. In such a case, the implementor has the option to try both port numbers in the boot stage.

When the client has no target name information at all, it may query the SLP discovery service with query string 4, and the service answers with a list of the iSCSI boot servers that the client is allowed to access. Alternatively it may query the iSNS discovery service to verify whether the targets in a particular Discovery Domain are bootable. If the list is empty, the subsequent actions are left to the discretion of the implementor. Otherwise the client may contact any iSCSI boot server in the list, and the order in which the servers are contacted is also left to the discretion of the implementor.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the DHCP or BOOTP server knows only the name of the disk, not where it lives. The client then asks a directory service, either SLP or iSNS, to turn that name into an address and a port. If it does not even have a name, it asks the directory for a list of servers it may use.

sections.title: The Boot Stage
sections.content:
Once the client has obtained the minimum information needed to open an iSCSI session with the boot server, the actual booting process can start.

The actual sequence of iSCSI commands needed to complete the boot process is left to the implementor. The RFC gives the reason: the requirements of different vendors and equipment vary, which makes it difficult to specify a common subset of the iSCSI standard that would be acceptable to everybody.

The iSCSI session established for the boot may be taken over by the booted software in the client.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the client knows where the disk is, it opens an iSCSI session and boots. The RFC does not fix the sequence of iSCSI commands for this step, because no common subset of the standard suits every vendor.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security discussion is centered on securing the communication involved in the iSCSI boot process. Applying credentials to a boot image loaded through the iSCSI boot mechanism is outside the scope of the document.

One key difference between the iSCSI boot mechanism and BOOTP-based image loading is that the identity of a boot image may not be known when the boot stage starts. The identity of certain boot images and their locations are known only after the contents of a boot disk exposed by the iSCSI boot service are examined. Images themselves may recursively load other images, based on both hardware configurations and user input. The practical answer the RFC gives is that each image loading program should verify the image it is about to load, using a mechanism of its own choice.

Enabling iSCSI boot creates a critical operational dependence on an external system, with obvious security implications, so administrator awareness of this enablement is extremely important. iSCSI boot SHOULD NOT be enabled, or put high in the boot order, without an explicit administrative action.

In all phases of the boot process, the client must ensure that a server is authorized to send it certain information. That means the authenticated identity of a server must have an authorization indication. A list of authorized servers can be pre-configured into a client, or the list can be downloaded in an authenticated form from a prior stage in the boot process.

The software stage SHOULD NOT be involved in a secure iSCSI boot process. Securing the loading of that software adds complexity, and the RFC notes that authentication and integrity protection for downloaded boot software has proven to be difficult and complex because of administrative issues and the limitations of the BIOS environment. It is therefore assumed that all the necessary software is resident on the client.

If the DHCP stage is implemented using the DHCP protocol, the client SHOULD implement DHCP authentication, and an administration interface SHOULD be provided for configuring those credentials, both when the network interface is on the motherboard and when it is removable. DHCP authentication is focused on intra-domain authentication, which is assumed to be enough for iSCSI boot scenarios. The reply from the DHCP server SHOULD include the serverName in IPv4 or IPv6 format, so that the boot does not have to rely on a DNS server for resolving names or on a discovery service entity to look up target names. That reduces the number of entities involved in the secure boot.

If the discovery service stage uses SLP, the client SHOULD provide IPsec support, marked as optional to use, for the SLP protocol. If the stage uses iSNS, the client SHOULD provide IPsec support, marked as optional to use, for the iSNS protocol. When SLP or iSNS is used to distribute security policy or configuration information, per-packet data origin authentication, integrity and replay protection SHOULD be used at a minimum.

For the final communication between the client and the boot server in the boot stage, IPsec and in-band authentication SHOULD be implemented according to the guidelines in the main iSCSI specification. Due to memory constraints, boot clients are expected to support only pre-shared key authentication in IKE, and where the host IP address is assigned dynamically, IKE main mode SHOULD NOT be used. Regardless of how the parameters in the earlier stages were obtained, the iSCSI boot session is vulnerable as any iSCSI session, so security for this session SHOULD be configured and used according to the same guidelines. A boot image that inherits an iSCSI session from a previously loaded boot image also inherits the security properties of that session.
sections.plainLanguage: Booting from the network means trusting whoever answers. The client should check that a server is allowed to send it information, and an administrator should turn the feature on deliberately. A step where the client fetches its own software should stay out of a secure boot.

viz.caption: THE FOUR BOOT STAGES (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC)

messages.label: DHCP request
messages.note: The client asks for an address and for information about its boot device.

messages.label: DHCP reply
messages.note: The reply may carry a Root Path string that starts with iscsi:.

messages.label: SLP or iSNS query
messages.note: Used when the client has the target name but not the address.

messages.label: Address and port
messages.note: The service resolves the target name to an IP address and a port.

messages.label: iSCSI session
messages.note: The client opens the session and boots from the server.

viz.caption: THE ROOT PATH STRING COMPOSITION FROM RFC 4173
THE FIVE FIELDS OF THE ROOT PATH STRING

items.title: servername
items.text: Optional. A domain name, a literal IPv4 address or a literal IPv6 address. Name compression must not be used.

items.title: protocol
items.text: Optional. Decimal transport number, default 6 for TCP, the only transport approved for iSCSI.

items.title: port
items.text: Optional. Decimal port of the boot server, defaulting to the well-known iSCSI port.

items.title: LUN
items.text: Optional. Four groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by hyphens. Blank means LUN 0.

items.title: targetname
items.text: Required. The iSCSI Name that uniquely identifies the target.

viz.caption: THE LUN FIELD: FOUR GROUPS OF FOUR HEX DIGITS, 8 BYTES

fields.name: Group 1
fields.desc: First group of four hexadecimal digits.

fields.name: Group 2
fields.desc: Second group of four hexadecimal digits.

fields.name: Group 3
fields.desc: Third group of four hexadecimal digits.

fields.name: Group 4
fields.desc: Fourth group of four hexadecimal digits.
